SAN DIEGO COUNTY – The merging of companies though acquisition activity is more than a blending of products or services and the teams that produce them, it is also a blending of two financial ledgers – ledgers that are governed by laws and meticulously prepared by accountants.


Accounting for companies considering or preparing for M&A activity changed at the beginning of this year as many of the new or extended tax provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act went into effect Jan. 1.


“The One Big Beautiful Bill made permanent or expanded several provisions that have a positive effect on M&A deals,” CBIZ San Diego Office Managing Director Stuart Starr and Managing Director of Tax Tim Willis said in a joint response to questions sent by the San Diego Business Journal.


Among the beneficial provisions in the bill is a 100% bonus depreciation on new and used property that allows companies to immediately deduct the full cost of eligible business assets in the year they are placed in service, rather than writing them off over many years. During mergers and acquisitions, the bonus depreciation boosts after-tax cash flow, increases the present value of tax shields, and influences how deals are structured and priced.


The bill also restored the ability for companies to deduct research and development costs; included a more favorable interest expense limitation that allows depreciation, amortization and depletion to be added back in calculating adjusted taxable income; opened the possibility to claim 100% depreciation on real estate used for qualifying manufacturing; and renewed Qualified Opportunity Zone federal tax incentives designed to encourage long-term private investment in economically distressed communities.


“Those provisions can affect cash taxes, the value of tax attributes and, ultimately, the economics of a transaction,” explained Citrin Cooperman’s Mergers & Acquisitions Tax Practice Leader Nichol Chiarella and Transaction Advisory Services Partner Paddy King in a joint response to questions sent by the Business Journal.


> “For business owners,
> tax planning should begin long before a deal is contemplated.”


Stuart Starr
San Diego Office Managing Director,
CBIZ


Tim Willis
San Diego Office Managing Director of Tax,
CBIZ


“There are also significant changes to the Qualified Small Business Stock rules under Section 1202. For qualifying stock issued after July 4, 2025, the gross-asset threshold for a qualified small business increased from $50 million to $75 million, and shareholders may be eligible to exclude up to $15 million of gain on the sale of stock, among other changes,” Chiarella and King added. “For founders, investors and growing companies, those rules can materially affect after-tax proceeds from a future exit.”


According to LevitZacks President Jared Werner, the most significant aspect of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act isn’t its new provisions, it is that the bill made several provisions from the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act permanent, like the 100% bonus depreciation, immediate R&D expensing and a permanent federal income tax deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income.


“That permanence matters at the negotiating table because it lets buyers and sellers model future cash flows and valuation assumptions with real confidence, rather than planning around provisions set to expire,” he said.


“Accelerated depreciation and immediate R&D expensing can improve after-tax cash flow and make certain businesses more attractive to buyers, and improved interest deductibility strengthens the economics of leveraged transactions.”


Brandon Smith, a high-net-worth accountant in EisnerAmper LLP’s San Diego office pointed out that the new tax provisions, and those that were made permanent from the previous Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, “have made decision-makers more focused on the timing and structure of transactions than they were a year ago.”


“These changes can widen the gap between buyer and seller preferences regarding asset versus stock sale structures,” he said, adding that an important consideration for companies in an M&A deal “is that many states, including California, do not conform to all of these federal tax provisions, which can significantly affect the overall tax impact of a transaction.”


> “Bad news doesn’t get better with time.
> The financial reporting house should be in order well before due diligence begins.”
>
>
> Jared Werner
> President,
> LevitZacks


### More Accounting Considerations in M&A


According to CBIZ’s Starr and Willis, the One Big Beautiful Bill has “generally been viewed as favorable for investment and acquisitions,” but has also made tax planning and transaction structuring even more important considerations in M&A deals.


“Buyers and sellers are spending more time evaluating how tax attributes, depreciation benefits, interest expense limitations, and state tax exposures affect valuation and after-tax returns,” they said. “For business owners, tax planning should begin long before a deal is contemplated. Transaction structure, state tax exposure, entity type, cost segregation opportunities, tax impact modeling and purchase price allocation can all have a significant impact on the net proceeds received by sellers and the after-tax economics for buyers.”


Chiarella and King from Citrin Cooperman described the M&A transaction process as placing a company’s financial and tax reporting “under a microscope.”


“Buyers and their advisors will perform a Quality of Earnings (QofE) review, analyzing historical earnings, working capital, accounting policies, tax compliance, debt-like items and numerous other aspects of the business,” Chiarella and King said. “Issues that may have seemed relatively minor during ordinary operations can become significant during diligence.”


For companies that are exiting in an M&A, the best time to identify those issues “is before a buyer does,” they added.
Proper accounting before entering an M&A transaction is important to maximize value in the deal because as Smith of EisnerAmper points out, both buyers and sellers base the transaction on the financial statements of the company for sale.


“If the numbers do not hold up, valuations can decline, terms may be renegotiated, or the deal can fall apart during due diligence,” he said.


Werner of LevitZacks pointed out that buyers want financial statements from sellers that “hold up under real scrutiny, not ones that simply check a compliance box.”


“A qualified accountant helps management build that credibility by identifying and documenting normalized earnings, distinguishing recurring operations from nonrecurring or owner-specific items, evaluating working capital requirements, preparing for quality-of-earnings reviews, assessing tax exposure, and helping ownership understand the implications of different deal structures,” he added.


> “Issues that may have seemed relatively minor during ordinary operations can become significant during diligence.”
>
>
> Nichol Chiarella
> Mergers & Acquisitions Tax Practice Leader,
> Citrin Cooperman
>
>
> Paddy King
> Transaction Advisory Services Partner,
> Citrin Cooperman


### Accounting Pitfalls to Avoid in M&A


Bringing on a qualified accountant will build credibility for management only if it is done before an M&A transaction begins, according to Chiarella and King, who said a common mistake companies make “is waiting until a transaction is underway to clean up accounting or tax issues.


“Once diligence begins, the timetable becomes compressed and sellers have much less control over how an issue is discovered or presented,” they continued. “Companies contemplating a transaction should conduct their own financial and tax readiness assessment well before going to market.”


According to Werner, the second most common pitfall for companies in a transaction is “inadequate support” for key financial statement balances.


“Revenue recognition, customer agreements, inventory records, and balance sheet reconciliations will receive the most scrutiny because they directly affect earnings quality and cash flow expectations,” he said. “Bad news doesn’t get better with time. The financial reporting house should be in order well before due diligence begins.”


Starr and Willis pointed out several other common issues discovered during due diligence, including state nexus, accounting estimates, poor documentation, related party transactions, R&D tax credits, change in ownership issues (IRC Section 382), cross-country repatriations and employee classification.


“A great example is State nexus,” they said. “As companies expand into new states through remote employees, e-commerce, or customer growth, they may create income tax, franchise tax, payroll tax, or sales tax filing obligations without realizing it. These nexus issues are frequently identified during due diligence and can lead to purchase price reductions, escrows, or indemnification claims.”


Commingling personal and business expenses is also a common mistake of businesses that may be discovered during diligence, according to Smith.


“Owner-operated businesses often run personal expenses through the company, which can lead to discounted valuations and concerns about the reliability of the financial statements,” he said.


Smith advises involving a CPA one to two years ahead of engaging buyers for an M&A transaction to “help clean up the books, model various tax structure options, optimize state tax outcomes and develop an estate planning strategy.”


Citrin Cooperman’s Chiarella and King pointed out another frequent issue that arises in diligence for an M&A deal: insufficient support for EBITDA adjustments.


“Sellers naturally want buyers to understand unusual, nonrecurring or owner-related expenses, but those adjustments need to be credible and well documented,” they said. “Unsupported adjustments can undermine confidence not only in the adjustment itself but in the broader financial information being presented.”


Chiarella and King also see companies underestimating tax diligence.


“Sales and use tax, payroll and employment taxes, state income taxes, historical acquisitions, entity classification and other tax matters can create exposures that ultimately affect purchase price, escrows, indemnification or deal structure,” they explained. “Addressing those matters proactively generally creates a much better negotiating position.”


> “If the numbers do not hold up, valuations can decline, terms may be renegotiated, or the deal can fall apart during due diligence.”
>
>
> Brandon Smith
> HNW Accountant,
> EisnerAmper
